opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one I've been thinking about for a long time. The fundamental challenge with specialized accelerators is that you get tremendous performance and energy efficiency by tailoring the hardware to the application domain, but then you've shifted the burden onto the software. Somebody has to figure out how to map these high-level programs onto a very complex, very parallel piece of hardware, and traditionally that's been the job of compiler writers who spend years building heuristics and hand-tuned optimizations. That just doesn't scale when the hardware is changing every generation and the models are changing every few months.

So the way I think about it is in a couple of layers. First, you want the right abstractions. In our work, going back to things like Delite and Spatial, and then the dataflow work that led to SambaNova, the idea was that if you capture the program at a high level, in terms of parallel patterns like map, reduce, filter and so on, you preserve the information you need about parallelism and locality. You don't throw it away by lowering to sequential loops and then trying to recover it later. That gives you a much cleaner optimization space.

Then the question becomes, how do you search that space? The space of tilings, fusions, memory allocations, and placements onto a reconfigurable dataflow fabric is enormous, and the cost models are hard to write by hand. That's where machine learning becomes really useful. You can learn cost models from data, you can use learned search to explore mappings much more efficiently than exhaustive approaches, and you can adapt as the hardware evolves without rewriting all your heuristics.

And more recently, with large language models, there's an even more interesting opportunity. We've seen that LLMs can actually generate pretty good kernel code, and if you combine that with verification and feedback from actually running the code on the hardware, you get a loop where the model proposes optimizations, you measure them, and you iterate. I think the key is not to trust the model blindly, but to use it inside a system that checks correctness and measures performance. So it's really AI for systems helping systems for AI, a virtuous cycle, and I think that's going to be essential if we want specialized hardware to be broadly usable rather than something only a handful of experts can program.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized hardware can deliver energy efficiency, but does not identify energy constraints as driving the need for specialized accelerator architectures.

r002.rationale: It describes compiler writers’ work as difficult to scale, but does not identify compiler development as typically the main bottleneck in designing specialized accelerator systems.

r003.rationale: The response recommends checking and measuring LLM-generated kernels, but does not state that LLMs alone cannot effectively search the compiler-solution space.

r004.rationale: It describes a surrounding loop in which the model proposes optimizations, correctness is checked, performance is measured, and the process iterates—an agentic workflow for guiding LLM optimization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about for a long time, and I'd say the compiler problem is really the fundamental problem with specialized accelerators. Everybody focuses on the hardware, and the hardware is actually the easy part in some sense. You can design a chip that has enormous peak performance, but if you can't map real applications onto it efficiently, nobody is going to use it. We saw that over and over again, going all the way back to the early parallel machines, and it's still true today.

So the way I think about it is in a couple of layers. The first thing you have to get right is the abstraction. If you start from something like C or CUDA, where the programmer has already made a lot of decisions about how computation is laid out, you've thrown away the information the compiler actually needs. At Stanford, with things like Delite and Spatial, and then at SambaNova with the dataflow approach, we took the view that you want to start with a high-level, domain-specific description, something that preserves the parallel patterns, the maps and the reduces and the stencils, and then the compiler has a lot of freedom in how it maps those onto the architecture.

Now, once you've done that, the problem is that the design space is enormous. You've got tiling decisions, how you partition across compute units, how you schedule memory movement, how you fuse operators, what precision you use. For a reconfigurable dataflow architecture you're essentially doing a kind of place-and-route of the computation onto the chip. These are combinatorial problems, and the classical approach is to write a lot of heuristics, which take years to develop and tend to be brittle. Every time the hardware changes or a new model architecture comes along, your heuristics are out of date.

That's where I think AI comes in, and I'd break it into a few things. The first is using learned cost models. One of the hardest parts of a compiler for an accelerator is just predicting how long something will take. The analytical models are never quite right, and actually running every candidate on hardware is too slow. So you can train a model to predict performance from the program structure, and then use that to steer the search. We and others have shown that this can get you to within a few percent of hand-tuned code, and sometimes beat it, because the search explores corners a human wouldn't bother with.

The second is using learning for the search itself, so reinforcement learning or learned policies for things like fusion and scheduling, rather than exhaustive or greedy search. The third, and this is the more recent and more exciting direction, is using large language models directly in the loop. These models have seen an enormous amount of code, and they're surprisingly good at proposing kernel implementations, transformations, even reasoning about why something is slow. The way I'd frame it is that the LLM becomes a very capable but unreliable collaborator, and the compiler infrastructure becomes the thing that keeps it honest. You generate candidates with the model, you verify them for correctness, you measure them, and you feed that signal back. That closed loop is what makes it work. Without the verification you'd never trust it, and without the model you'd be stuck with the slow, human-designed heuristics.

The thing I'd emphasize is that this isn't about replacing the compiler. The structure, the intermediate representations, the correctness guarantees, those are more important than ever, because they're what let you safely let a learned component make decisions. What changes is where the knowledge lives. It used to be that an expert spent five years encoding their intuition into the compiler. Now a lot of that intuition can be learned, and relearned when the hardware changes.

And frankly, I think this is one of the places where AI could have its biggest impact on AI itself. If we can make it dramatically cheaper to build a good compiler for a new architecture, then the barrier to specialized hardware drops a lot, and you get a much healthier ecosystem than one where everything has to run on the one platform with the mature software stack.

r001.rationale: The response discusses performance, programmability, and hardware ecosystems, but does not identify energy constraints as the reason for specialized accelerators.

r002.rationale: It calls the compiler problem fundamental, says the hardware is the easy part, and emphasizes that applications must map efficiently for accelerators to be used.

r003.rationale: It describes LLMs as unreliable collaborators that need compiler infrastructure to verify candidates, measure them, and feed results back; it says the closed loop makes the approach work.

r004.rationale: It describes a surrounding workflow that generates candidates, verifies correctness, measures performance, and feeds that signal back to the model.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tremendous opportunity there, because a compiler for a specialized accelerator has to make a lot of choices. How do you partition the computation? Where do you put the data? How do you schedule operations so that you’re actually taking advantage of the hardware? Those decisions interact, and the space of possible solutions gets very large very quickly.

Traditionally, we’ve relied on compiler experts to develop heuristics for navigating that space. With machine learning, we can learn from the results of different choices and use that feedback to guide the search. You can imagine compiling a program, measuring how well it runs, and using that information to improve the next mapping.

The distinction I’d make is between correctness and performance. We still want the compiler to enforce the rules that ensure the program computes the right answer. AI can help us choose among valid implementations to find one that runs efficiently. That’s particularly appealing for specialized accelerators, where getting the mapping right is a big part of realizing the hardware’s potential.

r002.rationale: It describes compiler decisions as complex and says experts develop heuristics, but does not state that compiler development is typically the main bottleneck in designing specialized accelerator systems.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention LLMs or say they cannot effectively search compiler solutions.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe an agentic workflow or say one is needed for LLM-guided search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a tremendous opportunity there. When you build a specialized accelerator, you’ve created a machine with a lot of potential performance, but now the compiler has to figure out how to exploit it. How do you map the computation onto the hardware? Where do you put the data? How do you schedule the communication? Those choices interact, so it becomes a very large search problem.

Machine learning gives us a way to explore that space more intelligently. Instead of relying entirely on heuristics that somebody has written by hand, you can learn which mapping decisions are likely to produce good results and use that to guide the compiler. You can also learn cost models, because evaluating every possible configuration on the actual hardware is too expensive.

The interesting thing is that you’re using AI to improve the software that makes AI run efficiently. I see that as a combination of compiler knowledge and learning: the compiler provides the structure and ensures correctness, and learning helps it find better implementations.
